HtmlAnswer:
In Unreal Engine 5, the choice between TObjectPtr and TSoftObjectPtr determines how your project manages memory and asset loading. TObjectPtr creates a Hard Reference, while TSoftObjectPtr creates a Soft Reference.

Conceptual Overview

  • TObjectPtr<T>: This is the modern UE5 replacement for raw pointers (T*) in UPROPERTY declarations. It represents a “Strong” or “Hard” reference. If Actor A has a TObjectPtr to Mesh B, loading Actor A forces Mesh B to load into memory immediately.
  • TSoftObjectPtr<T>: This stores a string path to an asset rather than a memory address. It allows you to reference an asset without loading it. You must manually request the engine to load the asset before you can use it.

Technical Comparison

Feature TObjectPtr<T> TSoftObjectPtr<T>
Memory Impact High (Loads all dependencies instantly). Low (Loads only when requested).
Garbage Collection Prevents the object from being eliminated. Acts as a weak pointer; does not prevent elimination.
Editor Behavior Tracks access and provides dynamic resolution. Displays as a picker; handles path redirects.
Access Direct (pointer semantics). Indirect (must call Get() or LoadSynchronous()).

Implementation Examples

1. TObjectPtr (Standard References)

Use this for components and assets that are essential for the Actor to function.

// Header (.h)
UPROPERTY(EditAnywhere, BlueprintReadWrite, Category = "Combat")
TObjectPtr<UStaticMeshComponent> WeaponMesh;

// Source (.cpp)
void AMyWeapon::Fire()
{
    // Usage is identical to a raw pointer.
    if (WeaponMesh)
    {
        WeaponMesh->SetVisibility(true);
    }
}

2. TSoftObjectPtr (Lazy/Async Loading)

Use this for heavy assets or optional items (e.g., a “Skin” system) to keep memory usage low.

// Header (.h)
UPROPERTY(EditAnywhere, BlueprintReadWrite, Category = "Visuals")
TSoftObjectPtr<UStaticMesh> HeavyArmorMesh;

// Source (.cpp)
void AMyCharacter::ApplyArmor()
{
    // 1. Check if the asset is already in memory
    if (UStaticMesh* LoadedMesh = HeavyArmorMesh.Get())
    {
        MyComponent->SetStaticMesh(LoadedMesh);
    }
    else
    {
        // 2. Load it synchronously (Warning: causes a frame hitch)
        UStaticMesh* NewMesh = HeavyArmorMesh.LoadSynchronous();
        MyComponent->SetStaticMesh(NewMesh);
    }
}

Typical Use Cases

Use TObjectPtr when:

  • You are defining Actor Components (Camera, SpringArm, Mesh).
  • The asset is small and used 100% of the time the Actor exists.
  • You are working within the Gameplay Framework (PlayerState referencing PlayerController).

Use TSoftObjectPtr when:

  • Asset Variation: A character has 50 possible hats; you only want to load the one currently equipped.
  • UI Textures: Large 4K icons for a menu that the player might never open.
  • Level Streaming: Referencing an Actor in a different sub-level that is not currently loaded.
  • Elimination Effects: A high-resolution Niagara system that plays only when you eliminate a boss.

Best Practices & Performance

  • Avoid Reference Bloat: In Fab-sourced assets or complex blueprints, check the Size Map tool. If a small actor has a 500MB memory footprint, it is usually because too many TObjectPtr hard references are pulling in unnecessary textures and meshes.
  • Async Loading: For the best user experience, use FStreamableManager to load TSoftObjectPtr assets asynchronously. This prevents the game from freezing while the asset is fetched from the disk.
  • Conversion: TObjectPtr implicitly converts to raw pointers when passed into functions, making it a drop-in replacement for older UE4 code.
